newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece wants experts to discuss spats with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece wants experts to discuss spats with Turkey.

text.p: Greece, which came to the brink of war with neighbouring Turkey last year, proposed on Wednesday setting up a committee of experts to seek ways to resolve problems between the two countries.

Deputy Foreign Minister Yannos Kranidiotis said Athens favoured an exchange of views between academics on procedural issues relating to Greek-Turkish disputes, which have long soured relations between the two NATO members.
"(Such a discussion), aiming to draw up a joint report on how to face problems, would be useful," he told an economic conference.

Greece's suggestion comes only days after Athens turned down a proposal by the Dutch presidency of the European Union for the creation of a "Wise Men" commission to try to settle Greek- Turkish problems.
"This proposal entailed dangers because it would essentially appoint a third-party referee in relations between Greece and Turkey," Kranidiotis said, repeating Greece's objections.
He said Greece would discuss its counter-proposal with the Dutch presidency.
EU-member Greece has blocked Turkey's efforts to get closer to the 15-member bloc, citing what it sees as aggression from Ankara and a poor human rights record.
Athens has a long list of disputes with Ankara, including rights in the Aegean Sea, the divided island of Cyprus and minority rights in both countries.

Cyprus, which also wants to join the EU, has been militarily divided since 1974, when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third of the island after a short-lived coup in Nicosia, engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Greece and Turkey came to the brink of war over a deserted islet in Aegean last January. A clash was averted with last-minute U.S. intervention.
Western allies have since been trying to mediate to ease tensions but there has been almost no direct contact between the two countries.

Ankara has repeatedly called for direct dialogue to resolve differences. Athens has adamantly rejected this, saying it would never negotiate its borders, and wants Turkey to take its territorial disputes to the International Court at the Hague.
